query_text: At what temperature do notched PP blend specimens transition from ductile to brittle fracture, and how does this ductile-to-brittle transition temperature shift as recycled PP content increases?
draft:
The ductile-to-brittle transition temperature (BDTT) of notched polypropylene (PP) blend specimens is not a single fixed value; rather, it depends heavily on the blend's composition and the inclusion of impact modifiers. For example, pure PP has been shown to have a BDTT of 90 °C, but the addition of 20 wt.% rubber shifts this transition down to 42 °C [Paper111]. In other systems, such as PP blended with polyolefin elastomers (POE), the transition temperature varies with the specific elastomer used: PP/POE 8677 exhibits a transition temperature below -45 °C, whereas PP/POE 6202 transitions at approximately -20 °C [Paper33]. 

Regarding the effect of recycled PP, the provided excerpts do not contain sufficient information to determine exactly how the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature shifts as the recycled PP content increases. The retrieved texts do note that incorporating post-consumer recycled PP (PPr) generally reduces the overall ductility of the blend. While a blend with 25% PPr retains a favorable balance of properties and ductility, increasing the recycled content to 100% PPr leads to severe embrittlement, characterized by an 85% reduction in elongation at break due to oxidative and thermal degradation [Paper12]. However, the specific temperature at which these recycled blends transition from ductile to brittle fracture is not documented in the provided text.

To fully answer how the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature shifts with increasing recycled PP content, additional data is needed. Specifically, results from notched impact strength tests conducted across a wide temperature range on PP blends formulated with varying, controlled weight percentages of post-consumer recycled PP would be required to map the exact shift in the transition temperature.
